title: Filter a list of strings to those containing ONLY vowels (`matches("[aeiouAEIOU]+")`).
shortTitle: Filter a list of strings to those containing ONLY vowels

s1_definition.profdef: `String.matches(regex)` tests whether the whole string matches a pattern. `matches("[aeiouAEIOU]+")` is true only when the string consists entirely of one or more vowels, so filtering on it keeps vowel-only strings.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya keeps only the codes made up entirely of vowels and throws away any that contain even a single non-vowel.
s1_definition.oneliner: `filter(s -> s.matches("[aeiouAEIOU]+"))` keeps strings made of only vowels.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `String.matches(regex)` tests whether the whole string matches a pattern. `matches("[aeiouAEIOU]+")` is true only when the string consists entirely of one or more vowels, so filtering on it keeps vowel-only strings.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya keeps only the codes made up entirely of vowels and throws away any that contain even a single non-vowel.

**One line to remember:** `filter(s -> s.matches("[aeiouAEIOU]+"))` keeps strings made of only vowels.

sections.s2_technical:
`matches` anchors the pattern to the entire string — it is as if the regex had an implicit start and end anchor — so the whole string must satisfy it. The character class `[aeiouAEIOU]` matches a single vowel of either case, and the `+` quantifier requires one or more, so the string must be all vowels and non-empty.

Used in `list.stream().filter(s -> s.matches("[aeiouAEIOU]+"))`, it retains only vowel-only strings. A string with any consonant, digit, or space fails because that character has no match in the class. The empty string also fails because `+` demands at least one character.

The senior nuance is that `matches` compiles the regex on every call, so for a hot path over a large list I precompile a `Pattern` once and use `pattern.matcher(s).matches()`. I keep the vowel definition explicit in the class rather than assuming a locale, and I decide whether y or accented vowels should be included. Anchoring behaviour is the key distinction from `find`, which would match a substring rather than the whole string.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A code catalogue at the National Bank of India tags special vowel-only mnemonic codes, and a filter must extract exactly those.

This is exactly what matches with a vowel-only pattern does — it keeps strings composed entirely of vowels.

The code defines a `VowelCodeService.onlyVowels` method with a precompiled pattern and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: the codes "AEI", "aei", "AB", "oue", "a1".

Step 1: The precompiled vowel pattern is applied to each string with matches, anchoring to the whole string.

Step 2: "AEI", "aei", and "oue" consist entirely of vowels, so they pass.

Step 3: "AB" contains the consonant B and "a1" contains the digit 1, so both fail.

Step 4: The survivors are collected.

```
INFO: Vowel-only codes: [AEI, aei, oue]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ["AEI", "aei", "AB", "oue", "a1"]
    │ filter(s.matches("[aeiouAEIOU]+"))   ← whole-string anchored
    │ AEI ✓, aei ✓, AB ✗ (B), oue ✓, a1 ✗ (1)
    ▼
  ["AEI", "aei", "oue"]
```

```
  ═══ LLD — matches vowel-only ═══

  ┌─ whole-string regex ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ matches(regex): anchors to ENTIRE string (implicit ^ $)    │
  │ [aeiouAEIOU]+ : one or more vowels, both cases             │

  └───────────────────────────────┘

  1. stream().filter(VOWELS.matcher(s).matches())
  2. toList()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To keep only strings made entirely of vowels I filter with the matches method against the pattern vowel character class followed by a plus. The crucial behaviour of matches is that it anchors the pattern to the entire string, as if there were an implicit start and end anchor, so the whole string must be vowels for it to pass. The character class covers both upper and lower case vowels, and the plus requires at least one character, which also correctly rejects the empty string.

Any string containing a consonant, digit, or space fails because that character has no match in the vowel class. At the National Bank of India I used this to tag special vowel-only mnemonic codes in a catalogue.

The senior point I stress is performance and clarity. The matches method compiles the regex on every call, so on a hot path over a large list I precompile a Pattern once and reuse its matcher, which is exactly what I did here. I also keep the vowel definition explicit in the character class rather than assuming a locale, and I decide whether y or accented vowels belong. And I always remember the distinction from find — find would match a vowel substring anywhere, whereas matches demands the whole string qualify, which is what "only vowels" really means.
